claims.evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by live imaging data presented in multiple figures.

claims.claim: SARM1 is the central executioner of pathological axon degeneration, an early feature of many neurodegenerative diseases.
claims.source: SARM1 is the central executioner of pathological axon degeneration, an early feature of many neurodegenerative diseases (Figley and DiAntonio, 2020; Krauss et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: SARM1 is the founding member of the TIR-domain family of NAD+ hydrolases.
claims.source: SARM1 is the founding member of the TIR-domain family of NAD+ hydrolases (Essuman et al., 2018; Essuman et al., 2017), and a metabolic sensor activated by disrupted NAD+ homeostasis (Figley et al., 2021; Gilley et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: SARM1 is a metabolic sensor activated by disrupted NAD+ homeostasis.
claims.source: SARM1 is the founding member of the TIR-domain family of NAD+ hydrolases (Essuman et al., 2018; Essuman et al., 2017), and a metabolic sensor activated by disrupted NAD+ homeostasis (Figley et al., 2021; Gilley et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Activation of the SARM1 NADase depletes cellular NAD+ and initiates a metabolic crisis that ultimately leads to axon degeneration and/or neuronal cell death.
claims.source: Activation of the SARM1 NADase depletes cellular NAD+ and initiates a metabolic crisis that ultimately leads to axon degeneration and/or neuronal cell death (Essuman et al., 2017; Gerdts et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Loss of SARM1 is profoundly protective in animal models of multiple neurodegenerative diseases including nerve injury, peripheral neuropathies, traumatic brain injury, glaucoma, retinitis pigmentosa, and Leber congenital amaurosis.
claims.source: SARM1 is a compelling target for therapeutic intervention, as loss of SARM1 is profoundly protective in animal models of multiple neurodegenerative diseases including nerve injury, peripheral neuropathies, traumatic brain injury, glaucoma, retinitis pigmentosa, and Leber congenital amaurosis (Geisler et al., 2016; Gerdts et al., 2013; Henninger et al., 2016; Ko et al., 2020; Osterloh et al., 2012; Ozaki et al., 2020; Sasaki et al., 2020b; Turkiew et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claims.claim: SARM1 is a druggable target as an enzyme.
claims.source: Moreover, as an enzyme, SARM1 is a druggable target, and both small molecule inhibitors and gene therapeutics effectively block axon degeneration (Bosanac et al., 2021; Geisler et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Both small molecule inhibitors and gene therapeutics effectively block axon degeneration.
claims.source: Moreover, as an enzyme, SARM1 is a druggable target, and both small molecule inhibitors and gene therapeutics effectively block axon degeneration (Bosanac et al., 2021; Geisler et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: SARM1 NADase activity is essential for injury-induced axon degeneration.
claims.source: SARM1 and its NADase activity are essential for injury-induced axon degeneration, and the SARM1 enzyme is activated within 1–2 hr after injury in cultured DRG neurons (Sasaki et al., 2020a).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: The SARM1 enzyme is activated within 1–2 hr after injury in cultured DRG neurons.
claims.source: SARM1 and its NADase activity are essential for injury-induced axon degeneration, and the SARM1 enzyme is activated within 1–2 hr after injury in cultured DRG neurons (Sasaki et al., 2020a).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Axonal fragmentation occurs approximately 4–6 hr after injury in cultured DRG neurons.
claims.source: Axonal fragmentation occurs much later in this system, with axons fragmenting approximately 4–6 hr after injury.
claims.evidence: This statement describes a temporal observation in the experimental system.

claims.claim: Numerous molecular and cellular events occur in the time between SARM1 activation and axon loss, including calcium influx, mitochondrial stalling and depolarization, loss of ATP, and disrupted membrane integrity.
claims.source: Numerous molecular and cellular events occur in the time between SARM1 activation and axon loss, including calcium influx, mitochondrial stalling and depolarization, loss of ATP, and disrupted membrane integrity.
claims.evidence: This statement summarizes known events that occur during axon degeneration.

claims.claim: Hours after injury there is a large influx of calcium that precedes axonal fragmentation.
claims.source: Prior live imaging studies have demonstrated that hours after injury there is a large influx of calcium that precedes axonal fragmentation, and blocking this late calcium entry with EGTA inhibits axon fragmentation (Adalbert et al., 2012; Loreto et al., 2015; Vargas et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2000; Yong et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Blocking late calcium entry with EGTA inhibits axon fragmentation.
claims.source: Prior live imaging studies have demonstrated that hours after injury there is a large influx of calcium that precedes axonal fragmentation, and blocking this late calcium entry with EGTA inhibits axon fragmentation (Adalbert et al., 2012; Loreto et al., 2015; Vargas et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2000; Yong et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Loss of mitochondrial mobility in injured axons is SARM1-dependent.
claims.source: In SARM1 KO neurons expressing GFP, mitochondrial movement was unchanged 4 hr after injury. In contrast, the number of motile mitochondria declines precipitously between 2 and 4 hr after injury in SARM1 KO axons re-expressing SARM1.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing SARM1 KO neurons expressing GFP vs SARM1, shown in Figure 1A and B.

claims.claim: Loss of mitochondrial mobility in injured axons requires SARM1 NADase activity.
claims.source: Catalytically inactive SARM1(E642A) is expressed at similar levels to wild-type (WT) SARM1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but did not result in loss of mobile mitochondria after injury (Figure 1A and B). Hence, the loss of mitochondrial mobility in injured axons is not only SARM1-dependent, but also SARM1 NADase-dependent.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the lack of effect of catalytically inactive SARM1(E642A) on mitochondrial mobility, shown in Figure 1A and B.

claims.claim: Injury-induced loss of mitochondrial potential is SARM1-dependent.
claims.source: Injury-induced loss of mitochondrial potential is also SARM1-dependent (Geisler et al., 2019), and so here we investigated whether or not this effect also requires a functional SARM1 NADase.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Loss of mitochondrial membrane potential after injury requires SARM1 NADase activity.
claims.source: As with mitochondrial dynamics, expression of WT SARM1, but not SARM1(E642A), leads to a dramatic loss of mitochondrial membrane potential after injury (Figure 2C and D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing effects of WT SARM1 vs SARM1(E642A) on TMRM staining, shown in Figure 1C and D.

claims.claim: The SARM1-induced decline in cytosolic NAD+ levels either directly or indirectly influences bioenergetics inside the mitochondria.
claims.source: The finding that SARM1 NADase activity is required for loss of mitochondrial membrane potential suggests that the SARM1-induced decline in cytosolic NAD+ levels either directly or indirectly influences bioenergetics inside the mitochondria.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the requirement of NADase activity for mitochondrial depolarization.

claims.claim: Calcium influx into injured axons requires SARM1 NADase activity.
claims.source: Axons show no calcium rise in SARM1 KO neurons expressing either GFP or SARM1(E642A), but have a significant increase in calcium when expressing WT SARM1 (Figure 1E and F). Hence, the loss of calcium homeostasis in injured axons also requires SARM1 NADase activity.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing calcium influx (Fluo-4 staining) in SARM1 KO neurons expressing GFP, WT SARM1, or SARM1(E642A), shown in Figure 1E and F.

claims.claim: SARM1 enzyme activity is essential for not only axon degeneration but also for the major proximate events that occur in injured mammalian axons.
claims.source: Taken together, these findings support the view that SARM1 enzyme activity is essential for not only axon degeneration (Essuman et al., 2017), but also for the major proximate events that occur in injured mammalian axons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing NADase-dependence of mitochondrial and calcium changes, combined with prior citation.

claims.claim: Pre-incubation with the MPTP inhibitor Cyclosporin A (CsA) does not delay the timing of axon degeneration.
claims.source: In contrast to prior findings, we observed no delay in the timing of axon degeneration with CsA treatment (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by axon degeneration assays with CsA treatment shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: CsA treatment has no significant effect on the increase in intracellular calcium after injury.
claims.source: We also assayed the increase in intracellular calcium after injury and again found no significant effect of CsA (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium measurements with CsA treatment shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Incubation with 10 µM BAPTA to chelate intracellular calcium has no influence on the progression of axon degeneration.
claims.source: To further explore the role of intracellular calcium, we incubated DRG neurons with 10 µM BAPTA to chelate intracellular calcium for 30 min prior to axotomy. This treatment had no influence on the progression of axon degeneration (Figure 2C), and was also unable to fully buffer the influx of extracellular calcium that occurs hours after injury (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by axon degeneration assays with BAPTA treatment shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Internal calcium is not a major determinant of injury-induced axon degeneration in this system.
claims.source: These results indicate that internal calcium is not a major determinant of injury-induced axon degeneration in this system; however, it may play a role in scenarios where SARM1 is less potently activated (Li et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lack of effect of intracellular calcium chelation on axon degeneration.

claims.claim: Pre-incubation with 3 mM EGTA potently blocked injury-induced calcium influx and maintained morphologically intact axons for up to 48 hr after axotomy.
claims.source: In agreement with prior studies, we find that pre-incubation with 3 mM EGTA potently blocked injury-induced calcium influx and maintained morphologically intact axons for up to 48 hr after axotomy (Figure 2D and E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with EGTA treatment shown in Figure 2D and E.

claims.claim: The presence of EGTA from 0 to 2 hr after axotomy has no impact on the timing of axon fragmentation.
claims.source: The presence of EGTA from 0 to 2 hr after axotomy had no impact on the timing of axon fragmentation, while addition of EGTA 2 hr post-axotomy was as protective as treatment at the time of axotomy (Figure 2D and E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course experiments with EGTA shown in Figure 2D and E.

claims.claim: Addition of EGTA 2 hr post-axotomy is as protective as treatment at the time of axotomy.
claims.source: The presence of EGTA from 0 to 2 hr after axotomy had no impact on the timing of axon fragmentation, while addition of EGTA 2 hr post-axotomy was as protective as treatment at the time of axotomy (Figure 2D and E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by time-course experiments with EGTA shown in Figure 2D and E.

claims.claim: Late influx of extracellular calcium is critical for axon degeneration in DRG axons.
claims.source: Hence, late influx of extracellular calcium is critical for axon degeneration in DRG axons, a finding consistent with previous reports (Vargas et al., 2015; Witte et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EGTA timing experiments, supported by citations.

claims.claim: Severed axons develop prominent axonal swellings following extracellular calcium chelation.
claims.source: While these results are consistent with prior work highlighting the importance of extracellular calcium for axon degeneration, we did observe that severed axons developed prominent axonal swellings following extracellular calcium chelation (Figure 2D, red arrowheads).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the EGTA experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: Mitochondria potential is lost by four hours post-axotomy whether or not EGTA is present.
claims.source: We find that mitochondria potential is lost by four hours post-axotomy whether or not EGTA is present (Figure 2F and G).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by TMRM staining in axons with and without EGTA shown in Figure 2F and G.

claims.claim: EGTA treatment fails to maintain mitochondrial mobility after axotomy.
claims.source: Similarly, EGTA treatment fails to maintain mitochondrial mobility after axotomy (Figure 2H and I).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by mitochondrial movement assays with EGTA shown in Figure 2H and I.

claims.claim: Treatment with EGTA halts mitochondrial movement and disrupts mitochondrial depolarization after 4 hr even in the absence of injury.
claims.source: Indeed, treatment with EGTA halts mitochondrial movement and disrupts mitochondrial depolarization (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) after 4 hr even in the absence of injury, demonstrating that chelating extracellular calcium is not an effective method to maintain healthy axons, and instead disrupts normal axonal physiology.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments on uninjured axons treated with EGTA shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Immediately after axotomy, a first peak of calcium bidirectionally propagates along the axon from the injury site.
claims.source: Immediately after axotomy, a first peak of calcium bidirectionally propagates along the axon from the injury site (white triangle). This elevated intracellular calcium is rapidly cleared, demonstrating that calcium homeostasis functions normally at this time, and is consistent with prior work and the findings in Figure 2E that the initial influx of calcium does not contribute to axon fragmentation (Adalbert et al., 2012; Loreto et al., 2015; Vargas et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging of calcium with GCaMP6 shown in Figure 3B and Video 1.

claims.claim: The elevated intracellular calcium after initial injury is rapidly cleared, demonstrating that calcium homeostasis functions normally at this time.
claims.source: Immediately after axotomy, a first peak of calcium bidirectionally propagates along the axon from the injury site (white triangle). This elevated intracellular calcium is rapidly cleared, demonstrating that calcium homeostasis functions normally at this time, and is consistent with prior work and the findings in Figure 2E that the initial influx of calcium does not contribute to axon fragmentation (Adalbert et al., 2012; Loreto et al., 2015; Vargas et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the observation that the first calcium peak is rapidly cleared.

claims.claim: The initial influx of calcium does not contribute to axon fragmentation.
claims.source: This elevated intracellular calcium is rapidly cleared, demonstrating that calcium homeostasis functions normally at this time, and is consistent with prior work and the findings in Figure 2E that the initial influx of calcium does not contribute to axon fragmentation (Adalbert et al., 2012; Loreto et al., 2015; Vargas et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and data in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: After nearly 4 hours, there is a large second influx of calcium that precedes any obvious change in axonal morphology.
claims.source: After nearly 4 hours, there is a large second influx of calcium that precedes any obvious change in axonal morphology. Soon thereafter, the axon thins and small swellings appear, then the axon swellings enlarge, and finally the axon fragments (Figure 3B and C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by live imaging shown in Figure 3B and C.

claims.claim: The time to the appearance of the second calcium peak varies dramatically, from less than four hours to nearly 10 hr after axotomy.
claims.source: From analysis of 22 single axons, we found that the time to the appearance of the second calcium peak varied dramatically, from less than four hours to nearly 10 hr after axotomy (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of 22 single axons shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Once the second peak of calcium appears, the axon fragments soon thereafter, with degeneration occurring ~100 min after initiation of calcium influx.
claims.source: However, once the second peak of calcium appeared, the axon fragmented soon thereafter. The correlation between the initiation of the second peak of calcium and axon degeneration was very strong (Figure 3D), with degeneration occurring ~100 min after initiation of calcium influx.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by analysis of 22 single axons shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Neither the duration nor intensity of the second calcium peak is well correlated with the timing of axon degeneration.
claims.source: In contrast, neither the duration nor intensity of the second calcium peak was well correlated with the timing of axon degeneration (Figure 3E and F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by correlation analysis shown in Figure 3E and F.

claims.claim: The very tight correlation between the initiation of the second influx of calcium and axonal fragmentation is consistent with the hypothesis that this calcium triggers the final disintegration of the axon.
claims.source: The very tight correlation between the initiation of the second influx of calcium and axonal fragmentation is consistent with the hypothesis that this calcium triggers the final disintegration of the axon.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the strong temporal correlation observed in the data.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial movement stops before the influx of calcium in injured axons.
claims.source: As shown in Figure 4A and in contrast to expectations, mitochondrial movement stops before the influx of calcium. Analysis of this single axon shows that fewer mitochondria are moving 3 hr after axotomy (Figure 4B), and that all mitochondrial are stalled by 4.4 hr after injury (Figure 4B, inset). At this point, the GCaMP6 signal is unchanged from baseline, but begins to rise soon thereafter.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simultaneous imaging of mitochondrial movement and calcium shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Loss of mitochondrial mobility precedes calcium influx by ~25 min in injured axons.
claims.source: Quantitative analysis of single injured axons demonstrates that loss of mitochondrial mobility precedes calcium influx in each case, and this occurs ~25 min after mitochondria stop (Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of single axons shown in Figure 4B and C.

claims.claim: Loss of mitochondrial mobility in injured axons cannot be due to calcium influx.
claims.source: Hence, loss of mitochondrial mobility in injured axons cannot be due to calcium influx.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that mitochondria stop before calcium influx.

claims.claim: The drastic drop in mitochondrial potential occurs prior to the large increase in calcium in injured axons.
claims.source: In the example shown, the abrupt drop in mitochondrial potential occurs one frame prior to the large increase in calcium. To assess this across axons, we identified the time at which the TMRM and GCaMP6 signal showed the largest frame-to-frame variation (Figure 4F and G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1). We found that the drastic drop of TMRM intensity occurs one frame prior to the large increase in calcium in five out of seven axons (71.43%), while these changes occurred during the same frame in two out of seven axons.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simultaneous imaging of mitochondrial potential (TMRM) and calcium (GCaMP6) shown in Figure 4D-G.

claims.claim: In injured axons mitochondria begin depolarizing prior to the calcium influx.
claims.source: The images are taken ten minutes apart, and so these data indicate that in injured axons mitochondria begin depolarizing prior to the calcium influx (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the timing analysis of TMRM and GCaMP6 signals shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: The data demonstrate a sequence of events in which first mitochondria stop, then begin losing their potential, and after that calcium enters the axon which subsequently degenerates.
claims.source: Moreover, these data, in conjunction with the analysis of mitochondrial mobility and calcium influx above, demonstrate a sequence of events in which first mitochondria stop, then begin losing their potential, and after that calcium enters the axon which subsequently degenerates.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined temporal analyses of mitochondrial mobility, potential, and calcium.

claims.claim: The loss of ATP in injured distal axons is fully SARM1 dependent.
claims.source: The loss of ATP in injured distal axons is fully SARM1 dependent (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ATP measurements in wild-type vs SARM1 KO axons shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: PercevalHR gives a reasonable estimate of changing ATP levels in axons.
claims.source: Using HPLC to measure axonal metabolites, we previously demonstrated that a 2 hr treatment with 50 μM CCCP lowers ATP by ~60 % in DRG axons (Summers et al., 2014). The same CCCP treatment leads to an ~70 % drop in the fluorescence level of PercevalHR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that PercevalHR gives a reasonable estimate of changing ATP levels in axons.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing CCCP effects on ATP (measured by HPLC) and PercevalHR fluorescence, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In every axon, the percent drop in the ATP sensor is larger than the percent drop in the fraction of mobile mitochondria at 3.5 hr after injury.
claims.source: In every axon, the percent drop in the ATP sensor was larger than the percent drop in the fraction of mobile mitochondria (Figure 5B left), and there was a strong correlation between the extent of ATP loss and mitochondrial stalling (Figure 5B right; R2 = 0.61, n = 9).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by paired analysis of ATP and mitochondrial mobility shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: There is a strong correlation between the extent of ATP loss and mitochondrial stalling (R2 = 0.61).
claims.source: In every axon, the percent drop in the ATP sensor was larger than the percent drop in the fraction of mobile mitochondria (Figure 5B left), and there was a strong correlation between the extent of ATP loss and mitochondrial stalling (Figure 5B right; R2 = 0.61, n = 9).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The extent of ATP loss by 3.5 hr after injury is a strong predictor of when mitochondrial will ultimately stop moving in an injured axon.
claims.source: In other words, the extent of ATP loss by 3.5 hr after injury is a strong predictor of when mitochondrial will ultimately stop moving in an injured axon.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the strong correlation between ATP loss and time to mitochondrial stalling.

claims.claim: All results are consistent with the model that ATP loss causes loss of mitochondrial mobility.
claims.source: All these results are consistent with the model that ATP loss causes loss of mitochondrial mobility.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal and correlative relationships between ATP loss and mitochondrial stalling.

claims.claim: Calcium influx precedes phosphatidylserine exposure in injured axons.
claims.source: In the example shown, calcium rises first, followed by staining with Annexin-V, and soon thereafter the mRuby3 signal declines indicative of axon fragmentation (Figure 6A). Indeed, in all cells analyzed calcium influx preceded phosphatidylserine exposure, and occurred ~0.51 ± 0.04 (hr) prior to Annexin-V staining (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by simultaneous imaging of calcium (GCaMP6) and phosphatidylserine exposure (Annexin-V) shown in Figure 6A and B.

claims.claim: Calcium influx occurs ~0.51 ± 0.04 hr prior to Annexin-V staining in injured axons.
claims.source: Indeed, in all cells analyzed calcium influx preceded phosphatidylserine exposure, and occurred ~0.51 ± 0.04 (hr) prior to Annexin-V staining (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantitative analysis of timing shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The influx of calcium and/or the decline in ATP likely triggers the loss of membrane asymmetry during axon degeneration.
claims.source: Calcium can inhibit the ATP-dependent flippase that maintains phosphatidylserine on the inner leaflet (Bitbol et al., 1987; Soupene, 2008), and so the influx of calcium and/or the decline in ATP likely triggers the loss of membrane asymmetry during axon degeneration.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on known mechanisms of flippase inhibition and the observed temporal relationships.

claims.claim: Dextran-3kDa is only observed in fragmented axons, not in swollen axons.
claims.source: In uninjured neurons, cytosolic GFP fills the axon while the dextran is excluded (Figure 6C). After injury, axon swelling is apparent, and mitochondrial localize to these swellings (Figure 7—figure supplement 1). The swellings retain GFP and still exclude dextran. Later, discrete puncta of dextran appear in axonal fragments, and such fragments contain no visible GFP.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of GFP and dextran shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Axon swellings burst, releasing soluble GFP and allowing entry to the high-molecular-weight dextran.
claims.source: We interpret this as axon swellings that burst, releasing soluble GFP and allowing entry to the high-molecular-weight dextran (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that dextran appears in fragments that lack GFP.

claims.claim: By 4 hr after axotomy of wild-type neurons, dextran is present throughout the axons, indicative of a loss of membrane integrity.
claims.source: By 4 hr after axotomy of wild-type neurons, dextran is present throughout the axons, indicative of a loss of membrane integrity.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by dextran uptake experiments shown in Figure 6D and E.

claims.claim: In axotomized SARM1 KO neurons, dextran is excluded from axons for at least 48 hr.
claims.source: In axotomized SARM1 KO neurons, dextran is excluded from axons for at least 48 hr.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by dextran uptake experiments shown in Figure 6D and E.

claims.claim: When wild-type neurons are incubated with EGTA, injured axons still swell but dextran is excluded.
claims.source: Interestingly, when wild-type neurons are incubated with EGTA, injured axons still swell (arrowheads, Figure 6D), but dextran is excluded (Figure 6D and E).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by dextran uptake experiments with EGTA shown in Figure 6D and E.

claims.claim: Calcium is necessary for the loss of membrane integrity and the morphological transition from axonal swelling to fragmentation.
claims.source: Therefore, we conclude that calcium is necessary for the loss of membrane integrity and the morphological transition from axonal swelling to fragmentation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that EGTA blocks dextran entry and fragmentation.

claims.claim: Following activation of SARM1, NAD+ is cleaved and its levels drop rapidly.
claims.source: Following activation of SARM1, NAD+ is cleaved and its levels drop rapidly.
claims.evidence: This is part of the model presented in the Discussion, based on prior knowledge and the current study.

claims.claim: Upon robust NAD+ depletion, both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation will be impaired, and so ATP production will decline.
claims.source: Upon robust NAD+ depletion, both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation will be impaired, and so ATP production will decline.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known role of NAD+ in metabolism.

claims.claim: Loss of ATP impacts molecular motors, leading to the observed halting of mitochondria.
claims.source: This loss of ATP will impact molecular motors, leading to the observed halting of mitochondria.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known ATP-dependence of molecular motors and the observed correlation between ATP loss and mitochondrial stalling.

claims.claim: The loss of NAD+ and ATP likely disrupts mitochondrial homeostasis, leading to loss of membrane potential.
claims.source: Soon after mitochondria halt, they lose their membrane potential. Since this occurs before calcium increases, this cannot be due to calcium overload. Instead, the loss of NAD+ and ATP likely disrupts mitochondrial homeostasis.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal sequence and known metabolic requirements of mitochondria.

claims.claim: The loss of ATP is a likely culprit for calcium influx, as ionic pumps require ATP and their loss will lead to disrupted calcium extrusion, membrane depolarization, and calcium influx.
claims.source: We next observed influx of extracellular calcium. The loss of ATP is a likely culprit, as ionic pumps require ATP and their loss will lead to disrupted calcium extrusion, membrane depolarization, and calcium influx.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the known ATP-dependence of ion pumps and the observed temporal sequence.

claims.claim: Loss of ATP and calcium influx may both contribute to the externalization of phosphatidylserine.
claims.source: After this large influx of calcium, the subsequent exposure of phosphatidylserine to the outer leaflet of the membrane is likely due to the failure of lipid flippases to maintain asymmetry. Since these flippases are ATP-dependent and can be inhibited by calcium (Bitbol et al., 1987; Pomorski and Menon, 2006; Soupene, 2008), loss of ATP and calcium influx may both contribute to the externalization of phosphatidylserine.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on known mechanisms of flippase regulation and the observed temporal relationships.

claims.claim: The ultimate loss of membrane integrity requires influx of extracellular calcium, as EGTA blocks fragmentation of injured axons.
claims.source: The ultimate loss of membrane integrity, however, requires influx of extracellular calcium, as EGTA blocks fragmentation of injured axons.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the EGTA experiments showing blocked fragmentation.

claims.claim: Calcium influx is merely leading to the morphological destruction of axons that are already physiologically dead.
claims.source: While calcium influx has long been assumed to the be the essential final step in axon loss, our findings suggest instead that calcium influx is merely leading to the morphological destruction of axons that are already physiologically dead.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that EGTA-treated axons maintain structure but have dysfunctional mitochondria.

claims.claim: ATP loss is the likely point of no return for an injured axon, disrupting mitochondrial, calcium, and membrane homeostasis and thereby triggering axonal demise.
claims.source: Instead, our findings highlight ATP loss as the likely point of no return for an injured axon, disrupting mitochondrial, calcium, and membrane homeostasis and thereby triggering axonal demise.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the temporal sequence of events and the observation that ATP loss precedes all other dysfunctions.

claims.claim: Mitochondria are transported by ATP-dependent molecular motors.
claims.source: Mitochondria are transported by ATP-dependent molecular motors, and so we hypothesized that loss of ATP may cause loss of mitochondrial mobility.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial transport mechanisms.

claims.claim: Catalytically inactive SARM1(E642A) is expressed at similar levels to wild-type SARM1.
claims.source: Catalytically inactive SARM1(E642A) is expressed at similar levels to wild-type (WT) SARM1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), but did not result in loss of mobile mitochondria after injury (Figure 1A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Most ATP loss occurs between 3 and 4 hr after injury in bulk injured axons.
claims.source: Based on ATP measurements from bulk injured axons, we knew that most ATP loss occurred between 3 and 4 hr after injury (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by ATP measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Phosphatidylserine is preferentially found in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane in healthy membranes.
claims.source: In healthy membranes, phosphatidylserine is preferentially found in the inner leaflet of the plasma membrane.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about membrane lipid asymmetry.

claims.claim: In cells undergoing apoptosis and in degenerating axons, phosphatidylserine is exposed on the outer leaflet where it serves as an 'eat-me' signal to phagocytic cells.
claims.source: In cells undergoing apoptosis and in degenerating axons, phosphatidylserine is exposed on the outer leaflet where it serves as an 'eat-me' signal to phagocytic cells (Sapar et al., 2018; Segawa and Nagata, 2015; Shacham-Silverberg et al., 2018; Wakatsuki and Araki, 2017).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Calcium can inhibit the ATP-dependent flippase that maintains phosphatidylserine on the inner leaflet.
claims.source: Calcium can inhibit the ATP-dependent flippase that maintains phosphatidylserine on the inner leaflet (Bitbol et al., 1987; Soupene, 2008), and so the influx of calcium and/or the decline in ATP likely triggers the loss of membrane asymmetry during axon degeneration.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claims.claim: Most axonal swellings overlap with mitochondria in injured axons.
claims.source: After injury, axon swelling is apparent, and mitochondrial localize to these swellings (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by imaging of GFP and MitoDR shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A 2 hr treatment with 50 μM CCCP lowers ATP by ~60% in DRG axons.
claims.source: Using HPLC to measure axonal metabolites, we previously demonstrated that a 2 hr treatment with 50 μM CCCP lowers ATP by ~60 % in DRG axons (Summers et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Treatment with 50 μM CCCP for 2 hr leads to an ~70% drop in the fluorescence level of PercevalHR.
claims.source: The same CCCP treatment leads to an ~70 % drop in the fluorescence level of PercevalHR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), demonstrating that PercevalHR gives a reasonable estimate of changing ATP levels in axons.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by PercevalHR imaging with CCCP treatment shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The absolute timing of cellular events varies dramatically from axon to axon during degeneration.
claims.source: In this study, we used live imaging of single axons to monitor structural and physiological changes during axon degeneration. While the absolute timing of cellular events varied dramatically from axon to axon, the relative timing was quite consistent.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the single axon imaging experiments.

claims.claim: The relative timing of cellular events during axon degeneration is quite consistent across axons.
claims.source: In this study, we used live imaging of single axons to monitor structural and physiological changes during axon degeneration. While the absolute timing of cellular events varied dramatically from axon to axon, the relative timing was quite consistent.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the single axon imaging experiments.

claims.claim: Live imaging of single axons allows ordering of cellular events, which is not possible when averaging responses from many axons that are responding asynchronously.
claims.source: Hence, this method allowed us to order cellular events, which is not possible when averaging responses from many axons that are responding asynchronously.
claims.evidence: This is a methodological conclusion about the advantages of single axon imaging.

claims.claim: SARM1 is a mitochondrial associated protein.
claims.source: This is of particular interest because SARM1 is a mitochondrial associated protein and so alternate mechanisms of action are plausible.
claims.evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SARM1 localization.

claims.claim: An NADase-independent function of SARM1 was recently described in Drosophila for organelle stalling after injury.
claims.source: Indeed, such an NADase-independent function was recently described in Drosophila for organelle stalling after injury (Hsu et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Loreto et al. found that injury-dependent mitochondrial stalling in superior cervical ganglion axons did not depend on SARM1, although loss of mitochondrial potential did depend on SARM1.
claims.source: Previously, Loreto et al presented the even more surprising finding that injury-dependent mitochondrial stalling in superior cervical ganglion axons did not depend on SARM1, although loss of mitochondrial potential did depend on SARM1 (Loreto et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Hsu et al. demonstrated that injury-dependent organelle stalling can be SARM1-dependent but NADase-independent in Drosophila.
claims.source: Recently, Hsu et al. working in Drosophila demonstrated that injury-dependent organelle stalling can be SARM1-dependent but NADase-independent (Hsu et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Treatment with 3 mM EGTA for 4 hr decreases mitochondrial membrane potential in uninjured axons.
claims.source: Indeed, treatment with EGTA halts mitochondrial movement and disrupts mitochondrial depolarization (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) after 4 hr even in the absence of injury, demonstrating that chelating extracellular calcium is not an effective method to maintain healthy axons, and instead disrupts normal axonal physiology.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Pretreatment with 3 mM EGTA or 10 µM BAPTA decreases calcium influx after axotomy.
claims.source: Application of 3 mM EGTA and 10 µM BAPTA influence Calcium influx after axotomy. D) Pretreatment with 3 mM EGTA or 10 µM BAPTA decreases Calcium influx. Statistical analysis using a one-way ANOVA (F (2,15) = 19.04, p < 0.0001, n = 6 embryos) and Sidak's multiple comparison testing finds a decrease in calcium influx upon 3 mM EGTA (t = 6.109, p < 0.0001) or 10 µM BAPTA (t = 3.806, p = 0.0034) treatment.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the background knowledge about SARM1 as a NAD+ hydrolase that executes axon degeneration in neurodegenerative diseases, is activated within 1-2 hours after injury, and represents a therapeutic target. These claims summarize the established state of the field based on prior work.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C15 are well-supported by extensive citations to prior literature. These background claims accurately represent the current understanding of SARM1 function, activation, and therapeutic potential. The claims are appropriately attributed to prior work and provide necessary context for the current study.

results.result: Prior studies have identified defects in calcium, mitochondria, ATP, and membrane homeostasis in injured axons, but the asynchronous nature of bulk axon cultures has made it difficult to determine the temporal relationships among these events. The manuscript identifies this as a key gap that motivates the single-axon imaging approach.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5 and C16-C19 accurately describe limitations of prior work and establish the rationale for the current study. The claims are supported by appropriate citations and correctly identify that temporal ordering of events has been challenging with bulk culture approaches. This provides strong justification for the methodological innovation.

results.result: Loss of mitochondrial mobility, mitochondrial membrane potential, and calcium influx in injured axons all require SARM1 NADase activity, as demonstrated by comparing wild-type SARM1 to catalytically inactive SARM1(E642A) in SARM1 KO neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C21, C23, C25-C26, and C81 are well-supported by data in Figure 1. The use of catalytically inactive SARM1(E642A) as a control is appropriate, expression levels are verified by Western blot (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), and the experiments demonstrate NADase-dependence for all three phenotypes. The statistical analyses are appropriate with sufficient replication.

results.result: The SARM1-induced decline in cytosolic NAD+ levels either directly or indirectly influences mitochondrial bioenergetics, as evidenced by the requirement of NADase activity for loss of mitochondrial membrane potential.
results.evaluation: Claims C22 and C24 are supported by the data showing NADase-dependence of mitochondrial depolarization (Figure 1C-D) combined with prior knowledge (C22 cites Geisler et al., 2019). The inference that NAD+ depletion affects mitochondrial bioenergetics is reasonable given the known role of NAD+ in mitochondrial metabolism, though the mechanism (direct vs. indirect) remains to be determined.

results.result: Neither MPTP inhibition with Cyclosporin A nor intracellular calcium chelation with BAPTA prevents axon degeneration or significantly affects calcium dynamics after injury, indicating that intracellular calcium is not a major determinant of injury-induced axon degeneration in this system.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C30 are supported by data in Figure 2A-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The experiments appropriately test the role of intracellular calcium using two different approaches (MPTP inhibition and direct calcium chelation). The conclusion that intracellular calcium is not a major determinant is justified by the lack of effect on degeneration timing, though the caveat about SARM1 activation strength (C30) is appropriate.

results.result: Extracellular calcium chelation with EGTA blocks axon fragmentation when applied 2 hours or more after injury, but not when applied only during the first 2 hours, demonstrating that late influx of extracellular calcium is critical for axon degeneration.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 are well-supported by the EGTA timing experiments in Figure 2D-E. The experimental design appropriately tests the temporal requirement for extracellular calcium by varying the timing of EGTA application. The conclusion that late calcium influx is critical is supported by the data and consistent with prior literature (cited in C34).

results.result: EGTA-treated injured axons develop prominent swellings and lose both mitochondrial potential and mobility despite maintaining morphological integrity. EGTA also disrupts mitochondrial function in uninjured axons, indicating it does not maintain healthy axonal physiology.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 and C96 are supported by data in Figure 2D, F-I and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. The observation that EGTA blocks fragmentation but not mitochondrial dysfunction is critical for interpreting the role of calcium. The finding that EGTA is toxic to uninjured axons (C38, C96) is an important control that challenges the interpretation of EGTA protection as maintaining healthy axons.

results.result: Single-axon live imaging reveals two distinct calcium peaks after injury: an initial bidirectional wave that is rapidly cleared, and a second large influx occurring 4-10 hours after injury that is tightly correlated with axon fragmentation (~100 min later). The absolute timing varies dramatically between axons, but the relative timing is consistent.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C48 and C89-C91 are well-supported by single-axon imaging data in Figure 3 and Video 1. The analysis of 22 single axons provides sufficient statistical power. The strong correlation between second calcium peak initiation and fragmentation (Figure 3D) contrasts with weak correlations for duration and intensity (Figure 3E-F), supporting the interpretation that calcium influx timing is critical. The methodological innovation of single-axon imaging is well-justified.

results.result: Mitochondrial movement stops approximately 25 minutes before calcium influx in injured axons, demonstrating that loss of mitochondrial mobility cannot be due to calcium influx.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 are supported by simultaneous imaging of mitochondrial movement and calcium in single axons (Figure 4A-C). The temporal analysis clearly shows mitochondria stop before calcium rises in all analyzed axons (n=9). The conclusion that calcium does not cause mitochondrial stalling is logically sound based on this temporal ordering.

results.result: Mitochondrial depolarization begins prior to calcium influx in injured axons, establishing a temporal sequence where mitochondria first stop moving, then begin losing potential, and finally calcium enters the axon.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C54 are supported by simultaneous imaging of mitochondrial potential (TMRM) and calcium (GCaMP6) in Figure 4D-G. The analysis shows that in 5/7 axons the TMRM drop precedes calcium rise by one frame (10 min), with the remaining 2/7 occurring in the same frame. While the temporal resolution is limited (10 min intervals), the data support the conclusion that mitochondrial depolarization precedes or is coincident with calcium influx.

results.result: ATP loss in injured axons is fully SARM1-dependent, and the PercevalHR sensor provides a reasonable estimate of ATP changes in axons, as validated by comparison with HPLC measurements of CCCP-treated axons.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56, C82, C87-C88 are supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and 2. The validation of PercevalHR against HPLC measurements (C87-C88) is appropriate, showing ~60% ATP loss by HPLC corresponds to ~70% PercevalHR drop. The SARM1-dependence of ATP loss (C55) is clearly demonstrated. This establishes PercevalHR as a suitable tool for the subsequent single-axon ATP measurements.

results.result: ATP loss precedes and correlates with mitochondrial stalling in injured axons. At 3.5 hours post-injury, ATP loss is always greater than the loss of mitochondrial mobility, and the extent of ATP loss strongly predicts when mitochondria will stop (R²=0.76), consistent with ATP depletion causing loss of ATP-dependent mitochondrial motors.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C58, C60-C61, C73, and C80 are supported by single-axon imaging data in Figure 5. The paired analysis showing ATP loss exceeds mitochondrial stalling at 3.5 hr (C57) and the strong correlation between ATP loss and time to mitochondrial stopping (R²=0.76, C60) provide compelling evidence. The inference that ATP loss causes mitochondrial stalling via effects on molecular motors (C61, C73) is reasonable given established knowledge (C80) and the temporal/correlative data.

results.result: Calcium influx precedes phosphatidylserine externalization by approximately 0.51 hours in injured axons. The loss of membrane asymmetry is likely triggered by calcium and/or ATP loss inhibiting ATP-dependent flippases that maintain phosphatidylserine on the inner leaflet.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 are supported by simultaneous imaging of calcium and Annexin-V in Figure 6A-B (n=10 axons). The temporal relationship is clearly established. The mechanistic inference (C64) is reasonable given established knowledge about flippase regulation by calcium and ATP (C83-C85, supported by citations). However, the mechanism cannot be directly tested due to the calcium requirement for Annexin-V binding.

results.result: Loss of membrane integrity, as measured by dextran uptake, occurs only in fragmented axons and requires calcium influx. EGTA blocks dextran entry and prevents the morphological transition from swelling to fragmentation, demonstrating that calcium is necessary for membrane integrity loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 and C77 are supported by dextran uptake experiments in Figure 6C-E. The observation that dextran appears only in fragments (C65) and the interpretation of bursting swellings (C66) are reasonable. The EGTA experiments clearly show that calcium is required for membrane permeabilization (C69-C70), as EGTA-treated axons exclude dextran despite swelling. The conclusion is well-supported by the data.

results.result: The study supports a model where SARM1 NADase activity leads to an ordered sequence: NAD+ depletion → ATP loss → mitochondrial dysfunction → calcium influx → phosphatidylserine externalization → membrane permeabilization → fragmentation. ATP loss is identified as the likely point of no return, with calcium influx merely triggering morphological destruction of physiologically dead axons.
results.evaluation: Claims C6 and C71-C79 represent the main conclusions and mechanistic model. The ordered sequence is well-supported by the temporal analyses from single-axon imaging. The inference that ATP loss is the point of no return (C79) is supported by the observation that EGTA blocks fragmentation but not mitochondrial dysfunction. The mechanistic links (C72, C74-C76) are reasonable inferences based on established biochemistry, though direct causal testing is limited. The reinterpretation of calcium's role (C78) is a significant conceptual advance supported by the data.

results.result: Most axonal swellings overlap with mitochondria in injured axons.
results.evaluation: Claim C86 is supported by imaging data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 showing colocalization of mitochondria (MitoDR) with axonal swellings (GFP). This observation is consistent with mitochondrial stalling preceding swelling formation.

results.result: Prior work in Drosophila and mammalian superior cervical ganglion neurons has suggested NADase-independent or SARM1-independent mechanisms for mitochondrial stalling, motivating the current investigation of whether mammalian DRG neurons show NADase-dependent mitochondrial phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 accurately summarize prior work (supported by citations to Hsu et al., 2021 and Loreto et al., 2015) that raised questions about the universality of NADase-dependent mechanisms. This provides appropriate context for why the authors tested NADase-dependence in their system. The current study's findings (C20-C21, C23, C25) resolve this question for mammalian DRG neurons.

results.result: Pretreatment with 3 mM EGTA or 10 µM BAPTA decreases calcium influx after axotomy.
results.evaluation: Claim C97 is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing statistically significant decreases in calcium influx with both EGTA and BAPTA treatment (one-way ANOVA with post-hoc testing, n=6 embryos). This confirms that both chelators can reduce calcium influx, though only EGTA blocks fragmentation (likely due to differences in extracellular vs. intracellular chelation).
